story: DOE commits up to $150 million in Defense Production Act money to a second Railbelt intertie, Beluga to Healy, while the Air Force offers base land in Alaska for AI data centers

claims.claim: The U.S. Department of Energy announced on October 5th its intent to deploy Defense Production Act funding for a second high-voltage connection between Southcentral and Interior Alaska.
claims.verbatim: The U.S. Department of Energy announced its intent to deploy Defense Production Act (DPA) funding to develop a second high-voltage connection between Southcentral and Interior Alaska
claims.notes: Press release dated October 5, 2026. ABSENCE FINDING, read across two full fetches of the release: the phrases 'data center' and 'data centers' do not appear anywhere in it. The only military sentence is Wright's 'military expansion' line (C09). Any deck link between this line and data centers has to be framed as the deck's own juxtaposition and never as DOE's stated purpose. Corroborated by Your Alaska Link (C12) and the Alaska Beacon (C14 to C17).

claims.claim: The DOE funding for the Alaska Energy Authority's Beluga-Healy Transmission Project is up to $150 million.
claims.verbatim: The Alaska Energy Authority's Beluga-Healy Transmission Project combines up to $150 million in DPA funding with $268 million in non-federal funding
claims.notes: NEEDS SOFTENING. This is a ceiling ('up to') and an 'intent to deploy', not money disbursed. Write 'up to $150 million'. The Beacon headline says 'Feds approve $150 million', so keep DOE's own hedge. Corroborated by Your Alaska Link and the Alaska Beacon.

claims.claim: DOE says the project pairs its funding with $268 million in non-federal funding.
claims.verbatim: combines up to $150 million in DPA funding with $268 million in non-federal funding, representing a planned total investment of $418 million in Alaska's grid.
claims.notes: NEEDS SOFTENING. The Alaska Beacon reports the $268 million is not yet secured and 'could come from other federal grants, the state, or even AEA itself, through loans', which conflicts with DOE's 'non-federal' label (see killed). Suggested phrasing 'DOE counts on $268 million in non-federal funding' or 'the remaining $268 million has not been identified, according to the Alaska Beacon'. Arithmetic checks, 150 plus 268 equals 418.

claims.claim: DOE puts the planned total investment in the Beluga-Healy line at $418 million, a preliminary planning estimate.
claims.verbatim: The current project has a preliminary planning estimate of approximately $418 million.
claims.notes: NEEDS SOFTENING. DOE's own words are 'preliminary planning estimate', so write 'an estimated $418 million'. Also on the page 'a planned total investment of $418 million'. The Alaska Beacon reports the same total ('expected to cost $418 million altogether').

claims.claim: The Beluga-Healy project would build approximately 223 miles of new transmission line.
claims.verbatim: Approximately 223 miles of new transmission line connecting Beluga and Healy will be built.
claims.notes: Corroborated by Your Alaska Link, 'The planned line would run 223 miles from the Beluga substation'. It is a planned line, so write 'would run' or 'planned'. For comparison, the existing intertie is 170 miles (C23).

claims.claim: DOE says the new line would strengthen grid reliability for approximately 75 percent of Alaska's population.
claims.verbatim: lowering electricity costs and strengthening grid reliability for approximately 75% of Alaska's population.
claims.notes: NEEDS SOFTENING. This is an agency projection of benefit, and the release also claims 'lowering electricity costs' with no figure. Attribute it as 'DOE says'. The 75 percent is roughly the Railbelt's share of the state's population, and DOE gives no source for it.

claims.claim: DOE says $1 billion in federal funding has been appropriated for energy-related projects deemed critical to national security.
claims.verbatim: $1 billion in federal funding has been appropriated for energy-related projects deemed critical to national security.
claims.notes: The release credits this to 'the passage of the Working Families Tax Cut'. That is DOE's name for the law, so keep the attribution in DOE's voice. The $1 billion is the national pool, not Alaska's share. Up to $150 million to this project would be about 15 percent of it.

claims.claim: Presidential Determination No. 2026-10 identifies transmission lines, conductors, substations, and power-control and protection equipment as essential to national defense.
claims.verbatim: Presidential Determination No. 2026-10 identifies transmission lines and conductors, substations, and power-control and protection equipment as essential to national defense.
claims.notes: We did not fetch the determination itself. This is DOE's description of it.

claims.claim: Energy Secretary Chris Wright said the project will support the U.S. military expansion underway in Alaska as well as mining and other resource development.
claims.verbatim: This project will not only support the major U.S. military expansion currently underway in Alaska, but also mining and other resource development critical to our national security.
claims.notes: A targeted second fetch confirmed it verbatim. The first full-text pass showed only Wright's opening sentence, so the showrunner may want one more look before setting it as a pull quote. Wright's other quoted sentences are 'Supporting improvements to Alaska's transmission infrastructure with Defense Production Act funds reflects the Trump Administration's commitment to strengthening national security, improving grid reliability, and lowering electricity costs.' and 'This meeting, combined with briefings from Alaska Command, confirmed the need to support an expansion of Alaska's energy infrastructure.' He names military and mining, and not data centers.

claims.claim: Wright said that thanks to Senator Sullivan he received an extensive briefing from the Alaska Energy Authority during a visit to Anchorage in August.
claims.verbatim: Thanks to Senator Sullivan, I received an extensive briefing from the Alaska Energy Authority during my recent visit to Anchorage in August.
claims.notes: Matches the AEA deck presented to Wright and Sullivan, dated August 27th and 28th (C20 to C22). A targeted fetch confirmed the quote verbatim, with the same caveat as C09.

claims.claim: Assistant Secretary Katie Jereza of DOE's Office of Electricity said Alaska's grid needs another way to keep power moving.
claims.value: another way to keep power moving
claims.verbatim: Alaska's weather is unforgiving, and its grid needs another way to keep power moving. Beluga-Healy will provide that critical second route.
claims.notes: The full-text pass returned this quote verbatim.

claims.claim: The planned line would run from the Beluga substation through West Susitna and Willow to existing infrastructure in Healy.
claims.verbatim: The planned line would run 223 miles from the Beluga substation through West Susitna and Willow to existing infrastructure in Healy.
claims.notes: Byline Anthony Wright. This is a write-up of the Alaska delegation's announcement from Sullivan, Murkowski and Begich. We did not fetch the delegation release itself. The route detail is not in the DOE release. Attribute it as 'according to the Alaska delegation' and treat it as planned, not surveyed.

claims.claim: The Railbelt currently relies on a single transmission corridor between Southcentral and Interior Alaska.
claims.verbatim: the Railbelt, which currently relies on a single transmission corridor
claims.notes: Corroborated by DOE's framing of a 'second high-voltage connection' and 'critical second route' (C01, C11), and by AEA's own page describing the one Alaska Intertie (C23).

claims.claim: Alaska Energy Authority executive director Curtis Thayer said the new federal money will likely go toward engineering, planning and permitting.
claims.verbatim: with the new federal money likely going toward engineering, planning and permitting, said Curtis Thayer, executive director of the Alaska Energy Authority.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Beacon (James Brooks), via Yahoo News
claims.notes: NEEDS SOFTENING. Keep 'likely' and 'according to the Alaska Beacon'. The Beacon is the original record of an interview with Thayer. The Beacon's own URL (https://alaskabeacon.com/2026/10/05/feds-approve-150-million-for-second-power-link-between-interior-and-southcentral-alaska/) returns 403. The same sentence was read verbatim in https://alaskabeacon.com/feed/, with pubDate Tue, 06 Oct 2026 00:52:31 +0000, which is the evening of October 5th in Alaska. If federal money goes mainly to engineering, planning and permitting, the line itself is not yet funded.

claims.claim: Thayer said the announcement came as a surprise and that he did not know until Monday that AEA had won.
claims.verbatim: On Monday, Thayer said the announcement came as a surprise. He had heard last week that the state was in the running for a large grant
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Beacon (James Brooks), via Yahoo News
claims.notes: The page reports this as indirect speech, so do NOT put 'came as a surprise' in quotation marks as Thayer's own words. Write 'Thayer told the Alaska Beacon the announcement came as a surprise'. Also confirmed verbatim in the Beacon RSS feed. The Monday in question is October 5th.

claims.claim: Alaska's existing intertie was built in the 1980s and is used primarily to ship lower-cost hydropower and natural gas power north to Fairbanks.
claims.verbatim: Alaska's existing intertie was built in the 1980s and is used primarily for shipping lower-cost hydropower and natural gas power north to Fairbanks.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Beacon (James Brooks), via Yahoo News
claims.notes: Independently corroborated by AEA's Alaska Intertie page, which says it was 'Constructed in the mid-1980s' and carries 'Bradley Lake and economy power north into the GVEA system'. Bradley Lake is hydro, and the economy power comes from CEA and MEA. Prefer AEA's 'mid-1980s' (C25).

claims.claim: Most of Alaska's military bases use energy that flows through the intertie, according to the Alaska Beacon.
claims.verbatim: Most of Alaska's military bases use energy that flows through the intertie, and the state's Congressional delegation emphasized that fact as it lobbied for federal funding.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Beacon (James Brooks), via Yahoo News
claims.notes: NEEDS SOFTENING. Single source, so attribute it 'according to the Alaska Beacon'. It is consistent with DOE's 'major military installations' framing and with JBER, Eielson, Fort Wainwright and Clear all sitting on the Railbelt. The same sentence notes the delegation lobbied on this point.

claims.claim: DOE says the new line would give grid operators an additional pathway between Alaska's most densely populated communities and major military installations.
claims.verbatim: grid operators will have an additional pathway to move power between Alaska's most densely populated communities and major military installations
claims.notes: The release names no specific installation.

claims.claim: In a presentation to Secretary Wright, AEA listed the Beluga to Healy Transmission Line as under consideration among future opportunities.
claims.verbatim: Under Consideration · Transmission Beluga to Healy Transmission Line
claims.notes: BACKGROUND, from before the window. Read through the r.jina.ai reader of the AEA PDF. The extraction letter-spaces the label ('U n d e r C o n s i d e r a t i o n · T r a n s m i s s i o n'). The showrunner also extracted it with scripts/fetch_pdf_text.py. The cover reads August 28, 2026, presented by Josi Hartley, Director of Federal Programs. The page footers read 'August 27, 2026', and the file name says 2026.09.01. Use 'late August' to avoid the date conflict. The section title 'Future Opportunities' was reported by the reader. About five weeks later the project was a DPA award.

claims.claim: AEA described the Beluga to Healy line as adding transmission redundancy along the Railbelt corridor.
claims.verbatim: Adds transmission redundancy along the Railbelt corridor and can improve reliability across the interconnected system.
claims.notes: BACKGROUND, from before the window. Verbatim in a character-level extraction through r.jina.ai. The deck makes no mention of data centers in this entry.

claims.claim: AEA's presentation to Wright reported $348.9 million in total awarded DOE funding committed through AEA.
claims.verbatim: Total Awarded DOE Funding $348.9M $348,896,491 committed through AEA across Alaska projects and communities.
claims.notes: BACKGROUND, from before the window. The figure predates the Beluga-Healy award and does not include it. The same slide shows 'Leveraged Dollars $242.7M'. Do not add $150 million to it as if that made a new official total.

claims.claim: The existing Alaska Intertie is a 170-mile line between Willow and Healy owned by the Alaska Energy Authority.
claims.verbatim: 170-mile long
claims.notes: Evergreen agency page with no publish date shown, so date_of_source is the fetch date. Other fragments on the page are 'between Willow and Healy' and owned by the 'Alaska Energy Authority (AEA)'.

claims.claim: The Alaska Intertie is built as a 345 kV transmission line but operates at 138 kV.
claims.verbatim: 345 kilovolt (kV) transmission line
claims.notes: The same page says it functions 'at 138 kV'. Evergreen page, so date_of_source is the fetch date.

claims.claim: The Alaska Intertie was constructed in the mid-1980s.
claims.verbatim: Constructed in the mid-1980s with $124 million in State of Alaska appropriations
claims.notes: The Alaska Beacon says 'built in the 1980s' (C16).

claims.claim: The Alaska Intertie was built with $124 million in State of Alaska appropriations.
claims.verbatim: Constructed in the mid-1980s with $124 million in State of Alaska appropriations
claims.notes: This is in 1980s dollars. Do not compare it directly with the $418 million estimate without an inflation note.

claims.claim: The Alaska Intertie carries Bradley Lake and economy power north into the Golden Valley Electric Association system.
claims.verbatim: Bradley Lake and economy power north into the GVEA system
claims.notes: The page says the economy power is supplied by Chugach Electric Association and Matanuska Electric Association, and that the Intertie joins GVEA with southcentral Alaska utilities.

claims.claim: The Pentagon has offered to lease about 4,700 acres of government land in Alaska to private companies for data centers.
claims.verbatim: The Pentagon has offered to lease about 4,700 acres of government land in the state to private companies, though no projects have been awarded yet.
claims.notes: Independently corroborated by the Department of the Air Force's own article (C31), 'approximately 4,700 acres of underutilized land'. WHRO says sites are being considered in Anchorage, Healy and Fairbanks.

claims.claim: As of September 28th, no Alaska military data center lease projects had been awarded, according to the American Homefront Project.
claims.verbatim: The Pentagon has offered to lease about 4,700 acres of government land in the state to private companies, though no projects have been awarded yet.
claims.notes: NEEDS SOFTENING. This is a status as of publication from a single outlet. HigherGov shows the solicitation was last updated July 14th with no award listed, which is consistent with it. Write 'no projects had been awarded as of late September, according to the American Homefront Project'.

claims.claim: Senator Lisa Murkowski said she is not a proponent of data centers at JBER or Alaska's interior installations because of an insecure energy base.
claims.verbatim: I am not a proponent of data centers down at JBER or at our interior installations because we are not able to support them because of an insecure energy base at this time.
claims.notes: Confirmed verbatim in a character-level fetch. The quote contains 'not able to', not 'cannot', so it passes the house rule as written. The article adds that she 'doesn't support bringing data centers to Alaska until that question is answered'. The page does not give the date or venue of her remark. Attribute it 'Murkowski told the American Homefront Project' or 'Murkowski said, according to the American Homefront Project'.

claims.claim: Fairbanks North Star Borough Mayor Grier Hopkins said whether local concerns about data centers reach the Pentagon is a different question from whether the bases listen locally.
claims.verbatim: I know that the bases at our level listen to what the impacts of the community would be. Whether that trickles up to the Pentagon is going to be a different question.
claims.notes: Hopkins quotes on the page, read in a character-level fetch, are 'Our community was buoyed by defense spending and infrastructure as the F-35 fighter squadron was placed here.', 'How our community grows and how it thrives is intimately intertwined.', and 'But here locally, the relationship is strong enough that we are listened to.' The introducing sentence is 'Fairbanks North Star Borough Mayor Grier Hopkins said his community's economy and culture strongly depends on the military.' Hopkins is not quoted opposing the leases.

claims.claim: The Department of the Air Force offered approximately 4,700 acres of underutilized land across JBER, Eielson Air Force Base and Clear Space Force Station for AI data centers.
claims.verbatim: The DAF is offering approximately 4,700 acres of underutilized land across Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson, Eielson Air Force Base, and Clear Space Force Station.
claims.source_outlet: U.S. Department of the Air Force
claims.notes: BACKGROUND, from before the window. Direct WebFetch returned 403. The text was read through the r.jina.ai reader of the same URL. The reader did not show the article's dateline, so date_of_source is INFERRED as April 2026, from the April 16th to 30th industry day and site visit dates in the article and the solicitation's April 10th posting on HigherGov. Cite it as 'this spring', not as a specific day. The article says the chosen developer handles financing, permitting, construction and operations.

claims.claim: The Air Force identified twelve parcels for potential AI data center development at the three Alaska installations.
claims.verbatim: Twelve parcels have been identified for potential development.
claims.source_outlet: U.S. Department of the Air Force
claims.notes: BACKGROUND. Read through r.jina.ai because the direct fetch returned 403. A first reader pass paraphrased it as 'Twelve sites', and a second, character-level pass gave the verbatim sentence above. Alaska's News Source (June 8th) says five of the parcels are at or near Eielson. The date is inferred, as in C31. Showrunner normalised value to the numeral 12 (the verbatim reads "Twelve parcels").

claims.claim: Proposals under Air Force solicitation AFCEC-26-R-0006 for AI data center development at JBER, Eielson and Clear were due June 29th, 2026.
claims.verbatim: Response Deadline: June 29, 2026, 5:00 p.m. EDT
claims.notes: BACKGROUND, from before the window. The verbatim is the deadline field as the fetch tool rendered it. The title is 'RFLP Artificial Intelligence (AI) Data Center Development at Joint Base Elmendorf Richardson, Eielson Air Force Base, and Clear Space Force Station'. Posted April 10, 2026, last updated July 14, 2026, agency AFICA. Independently corroborated by Alaska's News Source on June 8, 2026, 'With a June 29 deadline for interested companies to present their offers' (https://www.alaskasnewssource.com/2026/06/09/us-military-plans-lease-alaska-land-ai-data-centers-community-responds/).

claims.claim: The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Alaska District posted a request for information titled EIE490 Microreactor Synchronization, Eielson AFB, Alaska on October 2nd.
claims.source_outlet: SAM.gov (U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, Alaska District)
claims.notes: Solicitation number W911KB279A007, notice type RFI for market intelligence, NAICS 237130. The notice says nothing about data centers. Do not imply the microreactor serves a data center. It is a separate Eielson energy item that the deck can place alongside the data center leases, framed as context.

claims.claim: The Corps notice concerns a 45 MWth and 5 MWe nuclear microreactor initiative at Eielson Air Force Base.
claims.verbatim: a requirement for the design and construction on the installation of a 45MWth/5 Mwe nuclear microreactor initiative at Eielson AFB
claims.source_outlet: SAM.gov (U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, Alaska District)
claims.notes: 45 MWth is thermal and 5 MWe is electric. Do not present 45 as megawatts of electricity. An RFI is market research, not a contract award.

claims.claim: The Eielson microreactor work would extend the heating, power, communications and water systems to support plant operation.
claims.verbatim: by extending the heating, power, communications and water systems to support plant operation and distribution of general electrical and steam utilities to the installation.
claims.source_outlet: SAM.gov (U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, Alaska District)
claims.notes: The scope is design and construction of utility connections. The reactor itself is not what this RFI procures.

claims.claim: Responses to the Eielson microreactor request for information are due October 16th at 2 PM Alaska time.
claims.source_outlet: SAM.gov (U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, Alaska District)
claims.notes: UTC offset -08:00 is Alaska Daylight Time in October, so 2 PM Alaska time is correct. This is a future date and in-window context.

claims.claim: UAF announced on October 5th that it joins a $6 million National Science Foundation project with UAA, Montana Technological University and the University of Wyoming.
claims.verbatim: The $6 million National Science Foundation-funded project brings together researchers from UAF, the University of Alaska Anchorage, Montana Technological University and the University of Wyoming.
claims.notes: Byline Kate Avery, dated Oct. 5, 2026. Sanity check against NSF awards 2614749, 2614751 and 2614750: 3,824,575 plus 913,037 plus 1,260,800 equals $5,998,412, which matches $6 million. No separate University of Wyoming award was found, so Wyoming's share presumably flows through one of these awards. The awards were made August 5th, before the window, while this announcement is in window.

claims.claim: UAF's portion of the project, led by environmental engineering professor Srijan Aggarwal, is supported by nearly $913,000.
claims.verbatim: Srijan Aggarwal, UAF professor of environmental engineering and a principal investigator on the project, leads UAF's portion of the work, which is supported by nearly $913,000 of the total award.
claims.notes: Matches NSF award 2614751 (C45), $913,037.

claims.claim: In the project, AI will predict how readily rare earth elements can be recovered and will drive controls that adjust bioreactor operation as conditions and energy availability change.
claims.verbatim: AI will support two connected efforts: predicting how readily rare earth elements can be recovered from different materials and developing controls that adjust bioreactor operation as conditions and energy availability change.
claims.notes: NEEDS SOFTENING. This describes planned research, not results. Write 'aims to' or 'will try to'.

claims.claim: The project is one of eight receiving a combined $39.9 million to strengthen research capacity across 16 jurisdictions.
claims.verbatim: It is one of eight projects receiving a combined $39.9 million to strengthen research capacity across 16 jurisdictions.
claims.notes: Single source, the university's own release, and the NSF announcement of the round was not fetched. NSF award records show the program is 'EPSCoR RII: Focused EPSCoR Col'.

claims.claim: NSF award 2614749 to the University of Alaska Anchorage is $3,824,575, with Brandon Briggs as principal investigator.
claims.verbatim: "awardeeName":"University of Alaska Anchorage Campus" ... "fundsObligatedAmt":"3824575"
claims.notes: The fetch returned the field values id 2614749, estimatedTotalAmt 3824575, piFirstName Brandon, piLastName Briggs. The verbatim joins two JSON fields. The title is 'Collaborative Research: FEC: Transformative Bioprocessing and AI-Driven Frameworks for Sustainable Critical Mineral Recovery'. The award date of August 5th is inferred from the sibling awards 2614750 and 2614751, which show date 08/05/2026. Background date, with the announcement in window. UAA is the lead institution according to the abstract.

claims.claim: NSF award 2614749 runs from September 1st, 2026 through August 31st, 2030.
claims.notes: A four-year award. The sibling awards 2614750 and 2614751 have the same dates.

claims.claim: The NSF award abstract says the project applies reinforcement-learning controllers within a bioprocess digital twin integrated with microgrid simulators.
claims.verbatim: applies reinforcement-learning controllers within a bioprocess digital twin integrated with microgrid simulators
claims.notes: The identical abstract appears in full raw JSON for awards 2614751 and 2614750. The abstract also says 'This use-inspired project establishes a Smart Bio-Refinery framework and Virtual Pilot Plant to transform microbial rare earth element (REE) recovery from domestic coal refuse and ash into a predictive, energy-constrained system.' The organism named is Shewanella oneidensis.

claims.claim: NSF award 2614751 to the University of Alaska Fairbanks is $913,037, with Srijan Aggarwal as principal investigator.
claims.verbatim: "estimatedTotalAmt":"913037"
claims.notes: Raw JSON includes "pdPIName":"Srijan Aggarwal", "fundsObligated":["FY 2026 = $913,037.00"], "date":"08/05/2026", and program 'Artificial Intelligence (AI), Critical Minerals & Materials, Biotechnology, EXP PROG TO STIM COMP RES'.

claims.claim: NSF award 2614750 to Montana Technological University is $1,260,800.
claims.notes: The PI is Robin J Bullock. Award date 08/05/2026.

stories_surviving: DOE's Defense Production Act money for a second Railbelt intertie, Beluga to Healy, and the AI data center land on the bases it would serve
NSF EPSCoR $6 million AI smart bio-refinery for rare earths from coal waste, UAA lead with UAF

killed.claim: Construction of the Beluga-Healy line isn't expected until after 2030 (Alaska Beacon).
killed.why: Single source, with no primary and no independent second source. It appears verbatim only in the Beacon story (Yahoo syndication and RSS feed, which are the same article). The DOE release and the Your Alaska Link delegation write-up give no construction timeline, and the latter was checked explicitly for '2030'. The rule says kill. It revives if AEA or a second outlet confirms it, or if it is run as the Beacon's own reporting with 'according to the Alaska Beacon' and the showrunner accepts single-sourced status.

killed.claim: In recent years the existing intertie has shipped coal-fired power south to Anchorage amid natural gas shortages (Alaska Beacon).
killed.why: Verbatim on the Beacon page, but single source, with no primary or second independent source fetched. AEA's Intertie page describes only power flowing north.

killed.claim: The remaining $268 million could come from other federal grants, the state, or AEA loans (Alaska Beacon).
killed.why: Verbatim on the Beacon page, but it conflicts with the primary source. DOE calls the $268 million 'non-federal funding', and the Beacon says some could come from other federal grants. It is unattributed speculation and single-sourced. The deck should say only that DOE counts on $268 million in non-federal funding and that the source is not identified (see C03).

killed.claim: The Army Corps draft supplemental EIS analyzes Donlin tailings dam releases of 5.4, 13.3 and 27 percent of total tailings volume, versus up to 0.5 percent in 2018.
killed.why: Verbatim on ADN (Alaska Beacon, Yereth Rosen, September 29th), but single-sourced. The primary SEIS was not reachable (USACE Alaska District page 403, donlingoldeis.com redirects to a DNR page that returns 404), and no second outlet was found. Also, the input framed these as dam failure scenario percentages. They are shares of the tailings volume released in modeled breaches, NOT probabilities of failure, and the deck must never present them as odds.

killed.claim: The planned Donlin tailings dam is 471 feet high.
killed.why: Verbatim on ADN ('471-foot-high dam'), but single-sourced, with no primary reached. Same blockers as above.

killed.claim: The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers prepared the Donlin draft supplemental EIS.
killed.why: Supported only by ADN, and the primary Corps page returned 403. Story 3 therefore has zero surviving claims and is dropped.

killed.claim: DOE's Beluga-Healy release cites AI or data center demand as a reason for the line.
killed.why: False by absence. Two full reads of the DOE release found no occurrence of 'data center' or 'data centers'. DOE names military expansion, mining and resource development. Neither the delegation write-up nor AEA's presentation entry mentions data centers. Only the American Homefront Project and Murkowski tie Alaska data centers to the energy base.
